description: Recruiters posted fake job ads on social media, typically offering security guard positions paying MX$4,000-12,000 weekly (roughly US$200-600) - well above market. Applicants were told to gather at designated bus terminals and were transported to Rancho Izaguirre. Authorities identified at least 60 pages used for this.
energy_note: A good wage, a bus station, and a van.

aspect: EXAMPLE - many did not know who was hiring
description: While some listings advertised CJNG positions openly, many survivors reported being unaware of cartel involvement until they arrived. A reported survivor described being picked up at a bus station under false pretences and trained for a month in weapons and fitness; those who refused or tried to escape were beaten, tortured and killed.
energy_note: He thought he was going to a guard job.

description: The ranch, known as 'La Escuelita', contained human remains and over 400 items of clothing, plus bone fragments and hundreds of shoes. Federal officials later said they had not verified mass incinerations beyond one body - an investigative gap recorded here rather than resolved.
energy_note: Four hundred sets of clothes, and a dispute about the ovens.

aspect: EXAMPLE - it was not the first sign
description: In 2024, 30 young people disappeared after attending fake job interviews in San Pedro Tlaquepaque, Jalisco.
energy_note: Thirty, the year before, the same way.

description: José Gregorio Lastra, 'El Comandante Lastra', allegedly in charge of CJNG recruitment, was arrested on 24 March 2025. The Teuchitlán mayor was detained in May 2025 and local police were flagged. In July 2025 a court sentenced 10 men to 141 years each for crimes linked to the ranch.
energy_note: A mayor, the police, and 141 years each.

aspect: Most recruitment is not forced, which is the harder fact
description: Experts describe three routes: volunteers drawn by pay and status - the bulk of members - targeted recruitment of ex-military and police as trainers, and forced recruitment. The DEA estimates CJNG at around 19,000 members. For a young man with ECO-001's options, the offer is rational.
energy_note: For most of them it was the best job available.

description: The postings are ordinary-looking job ads on ordinary platforms, which is what makes the warning impossible to give usefully: there is no visible marker distinguishing the trap from the real vacancy.
energy_note: It looks exactly like a job advert, because it is one.

description: ECO-001's minimum wage against MX$4,000-12,000 a week explains the response rate entirely. The recruitment works because the legitimate economy offers him less.
energy_note: Four times the legal wage, and he has a daughter.
